newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Deputy PM denies assault but says sorry.
newsitem.headline: NZ Deputy PM denies assault but says sorry.

text.p: New Zealand Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters apologised on Thursday for a late-night fracas with a fellow-politician who alleged the flamboyant Maori leader had been drinking.
Peters, in a radio interview, denied allegations by conservative MP John Banks that he abused and physically assaulted Banks in a corridor of parliament late on Wednesday.
"I didn't touch the man," he said.

"We were walking down the corridor side by side having a strong conversation. That's not an assault, that's not an abuse, and you'd have to get a forensic scientist to try and find anything that would back that up."
Later, in parliament, Peters acknowledged the two men had had a dispute which had "clearly upset" Banks.
"I wish to tender my apology to him unreservedly," he said.
Banks complained to the speaker of parliament but said he considered the matter closed after Peters's apology.
Peters was not available later to comment on a separate allegation that he had been drinking. But a spokesman for Peters told Reuters: "I believe he had not been drinking."
Peters became number two in the government last December and secured the key portfolio of Treasurer when he steered his New Zealand First party into a coalition with the conservative National Party.
Banks, a National MP and former cabinet minister, said: "I was assaulted. I was grabbed by the shoulder and close to the scruff of the neck and given one hell of a good shake and push."
He added that he had thought Peters was going to hit him.

"I really feared for that. Not because I am fearful of being knocked to the ground by him. I don't want to get involved in fighting with people around here, rolling around on the carpets with the deputy prime minister."
Banks alleged Peters had not been in control of himself, and said he should seek help for anger management and drinking.
"I don't know when someone is drunk, but I know when they have drunk too much. He swayed and staggered at me and then I could smell it all over him. And it was very, very strong."
Left-wing Alliance party leader Jim Anderton backed the allegations that Peters had manhandled Banks.
Anderton and Richard Prebble, leader of the radical free-market Act New Zealand, both lodged complaints with parliament's speaker.
Anderton told reporters: "I have been asked whether I thought alcohol was involved and the answer is yes'... I could smell the alcohol and from quite a distance, I might say."
